title: Working Safely Near Overhead Power Lines
summary: Cranes, aerial lifts, high lifts, and ladders that contact overhead power lines cause serious injury and death. This talk covers looking up, keeping 20 feet of clearance, and using spotters.
talking_points: Look up and locate all overhead power lines before starting work.
Ask your supervisor to confirm the power company has de-energized and grounded the lines. When in doubt, treat every line as energized.
Keep machinery, equipment, and loads at least 20 feet from energized, uncovered power lines. Stay at least 20 feet from covered lines too.
Use only nonconductive or insulated tag lines. Never store materials or equipment under or near power lines.
Use a spotter and run machines slower than normal near lines. Wind can sway lines and cut clearance.
Never touch or approach a person or machine that is in contact with a power line. Call 911.
site_hazards_to_check: Overhead power lines not identified or flagged before work starts
Cranes, lifts, ladders, or loads within 20 feet of power lines
Conductive tag lines in use near energized lines
Material or equipment stored under power lines
No spotter assigned when equipment works near lines, or uneven ground that could make a machine sway
discussion_questions: Where are the overhead lines on this site, and are they confirmed de-energized?
How do we keep every part of the machine and load 20 feet away?
What do you do if a machine contacts a line and the operator is still on it?

flags: RESOLVED: The nonexistent 29 CFR 1926.453(b)(3)(i) citation has been removed. All five citations in osha_standards now exist and are on point.

CITATION VERIFIED - 29 CFR 1926.1408: 'Power line safety (up to 350 kV) - equipment operations.' Correct primary standard for cranes/derricks near overhead lines; Table A / 1408(a)(2)(ii) sets the 20 ft minimum clearance when line voltage is unknown for lines up to 350 kV.

CITATION VERIFIED - 29 CFR 1926.416: 'General requirements' (Subpart K). 416(a)(1) prohibits work near energized parts unless the employee is protected; supports the 'treat every line as energized' point.

CITATION VERIFIED - 29 CFR 1926.600(a)(6): equipment working, traveling, or parking near overhead lines must keep clearance and may only reduce it after the utility confirms lines de-energized and visibly grounded. Matches the de-energize/ground and clearance talking points.

CITATION VERIFIED - 29 CFR 1926.453(a)(1): 'Aerial lifts.' Incorporates ANSI A92.2-1969 (including appendix), the source of aerial-lift minimum approach distances from energized lines. Legitimate hook for the aerial/high-lift portion. Minor note (non-blocking): (a)(1) is worded as a design-and-construction conformance requirement; the operational approach distances it pulls in come from the referenced ANSI standard rather than the CFR text itself.

CITATION VERIFIED - 29 CFR 1926.1053(b)(12): ladders used where the employee or ladder could contact exposed energized electrical equipment must have nonconductive side rails. Directly supports the ladder-contact hazard and talking points.

TOLERANCE CHECK PASSED: 20 ft minimum clearance is correct for lines of unknown voltage up to 350 kV per 1926.1408 Table A. Treating lines as energized until the utility confirms de-energized and visibly grounded, nonconductive/insulated tag lines, spotters, slower equipment operation near lines, no storage under lines, and do-not-approach/-touch a machine in contact with a line are all accurate. No numeric errors.

LEGAL/LIABILITY CHECK PASSED: guidance directs foremen to have the supervisor/utility confirm de-energization rather than making definitive safety guarantees; emergency instruction (do not approach, call 911) is appropriate. No overreaching claims.
